claim: glod-4 glyoxalase enzyme mutants exhibit significantly enhanced pharyngeal pumping compared to wildtype N2 animals
source: Our initial observations revealed that glod-4 glyoxalases enzyme mutants exhibit a significantly enhanced pharyngeal pumping than wildtype N2 animals (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A comparing pharyngeal pumping rates between N2 and glod-4 mutants

claim: The increase in pharyngeal pumping in glod-4 mutants is consistent from day 1 to day 3 of adulthood
source: This increase in pharyngeal pumping was consistent from day 1 (young adult, post-65 hr of timed egg laying) till day 3 of adulthood (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by time-course experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: glod-4 mutants show increased bacterial clearance after 72 hr compared to wildtype
source: We found increased bacterial clearance after 72 hr in glod-4 mutants.
evidence: Supported by food clearance assay data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Serotonin treatment increases bacterial clearance in both wildtype N2 worms and glod-4 mutants
source: Serotonin treatment increased bacterial clearance in both wildtype N2 worms and glod-4 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C

claim: Worms lacking tph-1 enzyme show decreased pumping compared to wildtype N2 worms
source: Furthermore, worms lacking tph-1 (tryptophan hydroxylase, an enzyme that catalyzes the formation of 5-hydroxy-tryptophan, precursor for serotonin) enzyme as well as tph-1;glod-4 double mutants which lacks serotonin (Dallière et al., 2017; Ji Ying Sze et al., 2000) show decreased pumping compared to wildtype N2 worms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citations to previous literature

claim: tph-1;glod-4 double mutants show significantly increased pumping compared to tph-1 single mutants
source: However, tph-1;glod-4 double mutants show significantly increased pumping compared to tph-1 single mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: glod-4 null mutation mediated increase in pharyngeal pumping is independent of serotonin signaling
source: These data suggest that glod-4 null mutation mediated increase in pharyngeal pumping is independent of the serotonin signaling (Dallière et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing increased pumping in tph-1;glod-4 double mutants compared to tph-1 single mutants, with citation to previous work

claim: Enhanced feeding in glod-4 mutant worms is mediated by endogenous accumulation of AGEs
source: These preliminary observations lead to the hypothesis that enhanced feeding in glod-4 mutant worms is mediated by endogenous accumulation of AGEs characterized previously (Chaudhuri et al., 2016; Golegaonkar et al., 2015; Morcos et al., 2008).
evidence: Hypothesis based on previous characterization of AGE accumulation in glod-4 mutants, supported by citations

claim: MG-H1 and CEL are potential MGO-derived AGEs that increase feeding in C. elegans
source: To this end, we explored AGEs such as MG-H1, CEL, CML, and F-ly as possible mediators of feeding and identified MG-H1 and CEL as potential MGO-derived AGEs to increase feeding in C. elegans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by screening data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: Feeding MGO alone is not sufficient to increase the pharyngeal pumping rate
source: Just feeding MGO was not sufficient to increase the pharyngeal pumping rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: 24 hr of MG-H1 (150 µM) treatment is sufficient to significantly increase pharyngeal pumping in wildtype N2 worms
source: Time course analysis in wildtype N2 worms treated with MG-H1 showed that 24 hr of MG-H1 (150 µM) treatment was enough to increase pharyngeal pumping significantly (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by time-course experimental data in Figure 2C

claim: A significant increase in bacterial clearance is observed after 72 hr of MG-H1 treatment
source: A significant increase in bacterial clearance was observed after 72 hr (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2D

claim: Treatment of glod-4 null mutants with MG-H1 does not further increase bacterial clearance or pharyngeal pumping
source: Also, note that treatment of glod-4 null mutants with MG-H1 did not further increase either the bacterial clearance or the pharyngeal pumping (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that MG-H1 and glod-4 null mutation increases feeding by overlapping mechanism.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, with inference about overlapping mechanisms

claim: MG-H1 regulates pharyngeal pumping rate in a dose-dependent manner
source: In addition, we also demonstrated that MG-H1 regulates pharyngeal pumping rate in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by dose-response experimental data in Figure 2E

claim: MG-H1 is the product of arginine modification by MGO
source: Since MG-H1 is the product of arginine modification by MGO (see Materials and methods), we used arginine as a negative control for our MG-H1 treatment.
evidence: Based on established chemical knowledge and synthesis methods described in Materials and methods

claim: No significant difference is observed between worms treated with arginine versus water versus phosphate-buffered saline
source: We did not observe a significant difference between worms treated with arginine versus water versus phosphate-buffered saline (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: glod-4 null mutants have increased MG-H1 levels compared to N2 wildtype
source: Since MG-H1 induces increased pharyngeal pumping (Figure 2C, D), we validated an increase in MG-H1 in the glod-4 null mutants compared to N2 wildtype using liquid chromatography–multiple reaction monitoring (LC–MRM) mass spectrometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: Supported by LC-MRM mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I

claim: glod-4 mutants exhibit significantly increased preference toward food source OP50-1 at days 1 and 3 of adulthood compared to wildtype N2 worms
source: In addition to food consumption, the glod-4 mutant exhibited a significantly increased preference toward food source OP50-1 at days 1 and 3 of adulthood compared to wildtype N2 worms (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by food racing assay data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J

claim: Wildtype N2 worms prefer exogenous MG-H1 compared to MGO when provided with bacterial food source E. coli OP50-1
source: Furthermore, we noticed that wildtype N2 worms preferred exogenous MG-H1 compared to MGO when provided with bacterial food source Escherichia coli OP50-1 (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by food racing assay data in Figure 2G

claim: The preference for MG-H1 over MGO is not observed in the glod-4 mutant background
source: We did not observe this phenotype in the glod-4 mutant background (Figure 2H), suggesting MG-H1 in food makes it more appealing for control worms.
evidence: Supported by food racing assay data in Figure 2H, with inference about MG-H1's effect on food appeal

claim: RNAseq analysis identified 20,277 genes in total
source: Our RNAseq analysis identified a total of 20,277 genes, of which 5035 genes were significantly changed (2237 upregulated genes and 2798 downregulated genes) in glod-4 RNAi knockdown worms compared to N2 wildtype.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis

claim: 5035 genes were significantly changed in glod-4 RNAi knockdown worms compared to N2 wildtype
source: Our RNAseq analysis identified a total of 20,277 genes, of which 5035 genes were significantly changed (2237 upregulated genes and 2798 downregulated genes) in glod-4 RNAi knockdown worms compared to N2 wildtype.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis

claim: 2237 genes were upregulated in glod-4 RNAi knockdown worms compared to N2 wildtype
source: Our RNAseq analysis identified a total of 20,277 genes, of which 5035 genes were significantly changed (2237 upregulated genes and 2798 downregulated genes) in glod-4 RNAi knockdown worms compared to N2 wildtype.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis

claim: 2798 genes were downregulated in glod-4 RNAi knockdown worms compared to N2 wildtype
source: Our RNAseq analysis identified a total of 20,277 genes, of which 5035 genes were significantly changed (2237 upregulated genes and 2798 downregulated genes) in glod-4 RNAi knockdown worms compared to N2 wildtype.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis

claim: The functional category of genes regulating feeding behavior was significantly upregulated in glod-4 knockdown worms
source: Gene set enrichment analysis showed that the functional category of genes regulating feeding behavior was significantly upregulated in glod-4 knockdown worms (>twofold enrichment score) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, red * marked GO category).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: 66 neurotransmitters and feeding genes were differentially expressed in glod-4 knockdown worms
source: Previous studies in C. elegans have documented the role of neurotransmitters in C. elegans feeding behavior (Avery and Horvitz, 1990; Chase and Koelle, 2007; Trojanowski et al., 2016) and we observed differential expression of 66 neurotransmitters and feeding genes (which comprises ~19% of the total feeding and neurotransmission-related genes in C. elegans) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3A and citations to previous literature

claim: The 66 differentially expressed neurotransmitter and feeding genes comprise approximately 19% of the total feeding and neurotransmission-related genes in C. elegans
source: Previous studies in C. elegans have documented the role of neurotransmitters in C. elegans feeding behavior (Avery and Horvitz, 1990; Chase and Koelle, 2007; Trojanowski et al., 2016) and we observed differential expression of 66 neurotransmitters and feeding genes (which comprises ~19% of the total feeding and neurotransmission-related genes in C. elegans) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on calculation from RNAseq data and known total number of feeding/neurotransmission genes

claim: Mutation in tdc-1 suppresses the enhanced feeding phenotype in MG-H1 treated animals
source: We found that mutation in tdc-1, the gene involved in synthesizing neurotransmitter tyramine, suppressed the enhanced feeding phenotype in MG-H1 treated animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, indicated by a black arrow and Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by suppressor screen data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Figure 3C

claim: tdc-1 is the gene involved in synthesizing neurotransmitter tyramine
source: We found that mutation in tdc-1, the gene involved in synthesizing neurotransmitter tyramine, suppressed the enhanced feeding phenotype in MG-H1 treated animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, indicated by a black arrow and Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of tdc-1 gene function

claim: tdc-1;glod-4 double mutant animals show suppression of increased feeding rate compared to glod-4 single mutants
source: We also confirmed suppression of increased feeding rate in tdc-1;glod-4 double mutant animals (utilizing two different tdc-1 allelic mutants n3419 and n3420) compared to glod-4 single mutants (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using two different tdc-1 alleles shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: Receptors for tyramine and octopamine are G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)
source: Receptors for tyramine and octopamine are well-studied G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (Gross et al., 2014; Pirri et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from cited literature

claim: Mutation in ser-2 suppresses enhanced feeding in MG-H1 treated animals
source: Observed results showed a mutation in ser-2 and tyra-2 suppresses enhanced feeding in MG-H1 treated animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, indicated by black arrows).
evidence: Supported by GPCR screening data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: Mutation in tyra-2 suppresses enhanced feeding in MG-H1 treated animals
source: Observed results showed a mutation in ser-2 and tyra-2 suppresses enhanced feeding in MG-H1 treated animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, indicated by black arrows).
evidence: Supported by GPCR screening data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: tyra-2;glod-4 double mutant strains show reversal of feeding phenotype
source: A similar reversal of feeding phenotype was observed in tyra-2;glod-4, and ser-2;glod-4 double mutant strains (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3E, F

claim: ser-2;glod-4 double mutant strains show reversal of feeding phenotype
source: A similar reversal of feeding phenotype was observed in tyra-2;glod-4, and ser-2;glod-4 double mutant strains (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3E, F

claim: MG-H1-induced overfeeding is mediated by tyramine signaling
source: Our findings support the idea that MG-H1-induced overfeeding is mediated by tyramine signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic suppression experiments showing tdc-1, tyra-2, and ser-2 mutations suppress MG-H1-induced feeding

claim: Knocking down pha-4 suppresses the increase in pharyngeal pumping induced by MG-H1 treatment
source: Knocking down pha-4 and elt-3 suppressed the increase in pharyngeal pumping induced by MG-H1 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, indicated by black arrows).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Knocking down elt-3 suppresses the increase in pharyngeal pumping induced by MG-H1 treatment
source: Knocking down pha-4 and elt-3 suppressed the increase in pharyngeal pumping induced by MG-H1 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, indicated by black arrows).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: The pha-4 gene is crucial for pharynx development
source: The pha-4 gene is crucial for pharynx development, and loss of pha-4 results in a morphological defect of the pharynx (Mango, 2007; Mango et al., 1994), therefore, we followed the results from elt-3 knockdown in elt-3 mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from cited literature

claim: Loss of pha-4 results in a morphological defect of the pharynx
source: The pha-4 gene is crucial for pharynx development, and loss of pha-4 results in a morphological defect of the pharynx (Mango, 2007; Mango et al., 1994), therefore, we followed the results from elt-3 knockdown in elt-3 mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from cited literature

claim: elt-3 is essential to increase pharyngeal pumping observed in glod-4 mutant worms
source: Analysis of pharyngeal pumping in elt-3;glod-4 double mutant showed that elt-3 is essential to increase pharyngeal pumping observed in glod-4 mutant worms (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4D showing double mutant phenotype

claim: Knockdown of elt-3 using RNAi feeding in glod-4 single mutants suppresses the pumping
source: Also, note that the knockdown of elt-3 using RNAi feeding in glod-4 single mutants suppressed the pumping (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: HOMER analysis identified the binding site of elt-3 on the tdc-1 promoter
source: To determine the role of elt-3 in the tyramine signaling pathway, we performed a HOMER (Hypergeometric Optimization of Motif EnRichment) analysis and identified the binding site of elt-3 on the tdc-1 promoter, which suggested elt-3 may potentially regulate tdc-1 expression levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by HOMER bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: elt-3 may potentially regulate tdc-1 expression levels
source: To determine the role of elt-3 in the tyramine signaling pathway, we performed a HOMER (Hypergeometric Optimization of Motif EnRichment) analysis and identified the binding site of elt-3 on the tdc-1 promoter, which suggested elt-3 may potentially regulate tdc-1 expression levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from HOMER analysis identifying elt-3 binding site on tdc-1 promoter

claim: tdc-1 mRNA levels are reduced in elt-3 mutant worms
source: This was further validated by reduced expression of tdc-1 mRNA levels in the elt-3 mutant worms (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E

claim: elt-3 expression increases moderately but significantly after MG-H1 exposure in wildtype N2 worms
source: Next, to check if the elt-3 expression is changed on exposure to MG-H1, we treated wildtype N2 worms with MG-H1 and quantified mRNA levels of elt-3. We observed a moderate but significant increase in the elt-3 expression (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F

claim: tdc-1 expression does not change significantly after MG-H1 exposure in wildtype N2 worms
source: Although tdc-1 and tyra-2 did not change significantly, expression levels of other receptors, tyra-3 and ser-2, increased significantly after MG-H1 exposure (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F

claim: tyra-2 expression does not change significantly after MG-H1 exposure in wildtype N2 worms
source: Although tdc-1 and tyra-2 did not change significantly, expression levels of other receptors, tyra-3 and ser-2, increased significantly after MG-H1 exposure (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F

claim: tyra-3 expression increases significantly after MG-H1 exposure in wildtype N2 worms
source: Although tdc-1 and tyra-2 did not change significantly, expression levels of other receptors, tyra-3 and ser-2, increased significantly after MG-H1 exposure (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F

claim: ser-2 expression increases significantly after MG-H1 exposure in wildtype N2 worms
source: Although tdc-1 and tyra-2 did not change significantly, expression levels of other receptors, tyra-3 and ser-2, increased significantly after MG-H1 exposure (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F

claim: ser-2 is necessary to mediate the increased pharyngeal pumping in response to MG-H1
source: Note that ser-2 is necessary to mediate the increased pharyngeal pumping (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by genetic data shown in Figure 3F

claim: elt-3 plays a key role in tyramine-induced feeding increase in response to MG-H1
source: Together, these experiments identified a key role for elt-3 in tyramine-induced feeding increase in response to MG-H1.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing elt-3 regulation of tdc-1 and its requirement for MG-H1-induced feeding

claim: Tyramine has been demonstrated to decrease pharyngeal pumping in wildtype N2 worms
source: Tyramine has been demonstrated to decrease pharyngeal pumping in wildtype N2 worms (Dallière et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on cited literature

claim: Exogenous treatment of tyramine significantly decreases pharyngeal pumping in wildtype N2 worms
source: Consistent with this finding, we found that exogenous treatment of tyramine significantly decreased pharyngeal pumping (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5A and consistent with cited literature

claim: Exogenous tyramine treatment rescues tyramine signaling in elt-3;glod-4 double mutants and increases pharyngeal pumping to levels similar to glod-4 single mutants
source: However, exogenous treatment of tyramine to rescue tyramine signaling in both elt-3;glod-4 and tdc-1;glod-4 double mutants shows a significant increase in pharyngeal pumping to the levels similar to that of glod-4 single mutants (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5B, C

claim: Exogenous tyramine treatment rescues tyramine signaling in tdc-1;glod-4 double mutants and increases pharyngeal pumping to levels similar to glod-4 single mutants
source: However, exogenous treatment of tyramine to rescue tyramine signaling in both elt-3;glod-4 and tdc-1;glod-4 double mutants shows a significant increase in pharyngeal pumping to the levels similar to that of glod-4 single mutants (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5B, C

claim: Exogenous tyramine does not increase pumping in tyra-2;glod-4 double mutants
source: Exogenous tyramine did not increase pumping in the double mutants lacking tyramine receptors such as tyra-2;glod-4 and ser-2;glod-4 (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5D, E

claim: Exogenous tyramine does not increase pumping in ser-2;glod-4 double mutants
source: Exogenous tyramine did not increase pumping in the double mutants lacking tyramine receptors such as tyra-2;glod-4 and ser-2;glod-4 (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5D, E

claim: Tyramine suppresses pharyngeal pumping in N2 wildtype worms but increases pumping in the glod-4 mutant background
source: These results strongly demonstrate that tyramine suppresses pharyngeal pumping in N2 wildtype worms; however, it increased the pumping in the glod-4 mutant background.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing opposite effects of tyramine in wildtype versus glod-4 backgrounds

claim: Tyramine signaling is necessary to mediate glod-4 mutant-dependent increase in feeding behavior
source: These data support the notion that tyramine signaling is necessary to mediate glod-4 mutant-dependent increase in feeding behavior.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and pharmacological experiments showing tyramine pathway requirement

claim: Accumulation of α-DCs in glod-4 mutants results in neurodegeneration
source: Accumulation of α-DCs in glod-4 mutants results in pathogenic phenotypes, including neurodegeneration and shortening of lifespan (Chaudhuri et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on previous characterization cited from Chaudhuri et al., 2016

claim: Accumulation of α-DCs in glod-4 mutants results in shortening of lifespan
source: Accumulation of α-DCs in glod-4 mutants results in pathogenic phenotypes, including neurodegeneration and shortening of lifespan (Chaudhuri et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on previous characterization cited from Chaudhuri et al., 2016

claim: Chronic accumulation of MGO leads to the build-up of AGEs in glod-4 worms
source: Here, chronic accumulation of MGO leads to the build-up of AGEs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I), thereby increasing feeding in glod-4 worms (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and feeding data in Figure 2

claim: Accumulation of MG-H1 significantly reduces the lifespan of N2 wildtype worms
source: Furthermore, accumulation of MG-H1 significantly reduced the lifespan of N2 wildtype worms; however, it did not further exacerbate the damage in glod-4 mutant worms (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: MG-H1 accumulation does not further exacerbate the damage in glod-4 mutant worms
source: Furthermore, accumulation of MG-H1 significantly reduced the lifespan of N2 wildtype worms; however, it did not further exacerbate the damage in glod-4 mutant worms (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The lifespan of glod-4 mutants is significantly increased upon inhibition of tyramine signaling in the tdc-1;glod-4 double mutation
source: The lifespan of glod-4 was significantly increased upon inhibition of tyramine signaling in the tdc-1;glod-4 double mutation (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by lifespan assay data in Figure 6A

claim: Lifespan increases significantly in the absence of tyra-2 in tyra-2;glod-4 double mutant animals
source: Lifespan increased significantly in the absence of either tyra-2 or ser-2 in double mutant animals (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: Supported by lifespan assay data in Figure 6B, C

claim: Lifespan increases significantly in the absence of ser-2 in ser-2;glod-4 double mutant animals
source: Lifespan increased significantly in the absence of either tyra-2 or ser-2 in double mutant animals (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: Supported by lifespan assay data in Figure 6B, C

claim: The lack of tyramine results in partial but significant rescue of neuronal damage in glod-4 animals
source: In addition to rescuing lifespan and feeding rate, the lack of tyramine also resulted in the partial but significant rescue of neuronal damage in glod-4 animals (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: Supported by neuronal damage quantification data in Figure 6D, E

claim: The Maillard reaction is a chemical reaction between amino acids and sugars
source: The Maillard reaction, a chemical reaction between amino acids and sugars, is exploited to produce flavorful food ubiquitously, from the baking industry to our everyday lives.
evidence: Based on established chemical knowledge

claim: The Maillard reaction is exploited to produce flavorful food in the baking industry and everyday cooking
source: The Maillard reaction, a chemical reaction between amino acids and sugars, is exploited to produce flavorful food ubiquitously, from the baking industry to our everyday lives.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of food chemistry

claim: The Maillard reaction occurs in all cells, from prokaryotes to eukaryotes
source: However, the Maillard reaction also occurs in all cells, from prokaryotes to eukaryotes, forming advanced glycation end-products (AGEs).
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge

claim: AGEs are a heterogeneous group of compounds resulting from the irreversible reaction between biomolecules and α-dicarbonyls
source: AGEs are a heterogeneous group of compounds resulting from the irreversible reaction between biomolecules and α-dicarbonyls (α-DCs), including methylglyoxal (MGO), an unavoidable byproduct of anaerobic glycolysis and lipid peroxidation.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge

claim: Methylglyoxal (MGO) is an unavoidable byproduct of anaerobic glycolysis and lipid peroxidation
source: AGEs are a heterogeneous group of compounds resulting from the irreversible reaction between biomolecules and α-dicarbonyls (α-DCs), including methylglyoxal (MGO), an unavoidable byproduct of anaerobic glycolysis and lipid peroxidation.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge

claim: C. elegans mutants lacking the glod-4 glyoxalase enzyme display enhanced accumulation of α-DCs
source: We previously demonstrated that Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking the glod-4 glyoxalase enzyme displayed enhanced accumulation of α-DCs, reduced lifespan, increased neuronal damage, and touch hypersensitivity.
evidence: Based on previous work by the authors

claim: C. elegans mutants lacking the glod-4 glyoxalase enzyme display reduced lifespan
source: We previously demonstrated that Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking the glod-4 glyoxalase enzyme displayed enhanced accumulation of α-DCs, reduced lifespan, increased neuronal damage, and touch hypersensitivity.
evidence: Based on previous work by the authors

claim: C. elegans mutants lacking the glod-4 glyoxalase enzyme display increased neuronal damage
source: We previously demonstrated that Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking the glod-4 glyoxalase enzyme displayed enhanced accumulation of α-DCs, reduced lifespan, increased neuronal damage, and touch hypersensitivity.
evidence: Based on previous work by the authors

claim: C. elegans mutants lacking the glod-4 glyoxalase enzyme display touch hypersensitivity
source: We previously demonstrated that Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking the glod-4 glyoxalase enzyme displayed enhanced accumulation of α-DCs, reduced lifespan, increased neuronal damage, and touch hypersensitivity.
evidence: Based on previous work by the authors

claim: glod-4 mutation increases food intake
source: Here, we demonstrate that glod-4 mutation increased food intake and identify that MGO-derived hydroimidazolone, MG-H1, is a mediator of the observed increase in food intake.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: MGO-derived hydroimidazolone, MG-H1, is a mediator of the observed increase in food intake in glod-4 mutants
source: Here, we demonstrate that glod-4 mutation increased food intake and identify that MGO-derived hydroimidazolone, MG-H1, is a mediator of the observed increase in food intake.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing MG-H1 treatment increases feeding and genetic experiments

claim: RNAseq analysis in glod-4 knockdown worms identified upregulation of several neurotransmitters and feeding genes
source: RNAseq analysis in glod-4 knockdown worms identified upregulation of several neurotransmitters and feeding genes.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The tdc-1-tyramine-tyra-2/ser-2 signaling pathway is essential for mediating AGE (MG-H1)-induced feeding in glod-4 mutants
source: Suppressor screening of the overfeeding phenotype identified the tdc-1-tyramine-tyra-2/ser-2 signaling as an essential pathway mediating AGE (MG-H1)-induced feeding in glod-4 mutants.
evidence: Supported by suppressor screen data and genetic experiments

claim: The elt-3 GATA transcription factor is an essential upstream regulator for increased feeding upon accumulation of AGEs
source: We also identified the elt-3 GATA transcription factor as an essential upstream regulator for increased feeding upon accumulation of AGEs by partially controlling the expression of tdc-1 gene.
evidence: Supported by genetic experiments and gene expression analysis

claim: elt-3 partially controls the expression of tdc-1 gene
source: We also identified the elt-3 GATA transcription factor as an essential upstream regulator for increased feeding upon accumulation of AGEs by partially controlling the expression of tdc-1 gene.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing reduced tdc-1 expression in elt-3 mutants and HOMER analysis

claim: The lack of tdc-1 suppresses the reduced lifespan observed in glod-4 mutants
source: Furthermore, the lack of either tdc-1 or tyra-2/ser-2 receptors suppresses the reduced lifespan and rescues neuronal damage observed in glod-4 mutants.
evidence: Supported by lifespan assay data in Figure 6A

claim: The lack of tyra-2/ser-2 receptors suppresses the reduced lifespan observed in glod-4 mutants
source: Furthermore, the lack of either tdc-1 or tyra-2/ser-2 receptors suppresses the reduced lifespan and rescues neuronal damage observed in glod-4 mutants.
evidence: Supported by lifespan assay data in Figure 6B, C

claim: The lack of tdc-1 rescues neuronal damage observed in glod-4 mutants
source: Furthermore, the lack of either tdc-1 or tyra-2/ser-2 receptors suppresses the reduced lifespan and rescues neuronal damage observed in glod-4 mutants.
evidence: Supported by neuronal damage quantification data in Figure 6D, E

claim: The lack of tyra-2/ser-2 receptors rescues neuronal damage observed in glod-4 mutants
source: Furthermore, the lack of either tdc-1 or tyra-2/ser-2 receptors suppresses the reduced lifespan and rescues neuronal damage observed in glod-4 mutants.
evidence: Supported by neuronal damage quantification data in Figure 6D, E

claim: An elt-3 regulated tyramine-dependent pathway mediates the toxic effects of MG-H1 AGE in C. elegans
source: Thus, in C. elegans, we identified an elt-3 regulated tyramine-dependent pathway mediating the toxic effects of MG-H1 AGE.
evidence: Inferred from the combined genetic, molecular, and phenotypic data presented throughout the study

claim: Understanding the elt-3-tyramine signaling pathway may help understand hedonistic overfeeding behavior observed due to modern AGE-rich diets
source: Understanding this signaling pathway may help understand hedonistic overfeeding behavior observed due to modern AGE-rich diets.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential implications of the findings

claim: In 1912, L.C. Maillard reported a reaction between glucose and glycine upon heating, resulting in the formation of brown pigments
source: In 1912, a French Chemist, L.C. Maillard, reported a reaction between glucose and glycine upon heating, resulting in the formation of brown pigments (Maillard, 1912).
evidence: Historical fact cited from Maillard, 1912

claim: The covalent bonds formed between carbohydrates and proteins during heating in a non-enzymatic browning reaction was named the Maillard reaction
source: Later, the covalent bonds formed between carbohydrates and proteins during heating in a non-enzymatic browning reaction was named the Maillard reaction (Jaeger et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Historical fact cited from literature

claim: Glycation is a part of the Maillard reaction during cooking which enhances the taste, color, and aroma of food
source: Glycation is a part of the Maillard reaction, or browning of food, during cooking which enhances the taste, color, and aroma of the food to make it more palatable (Maillard, 1912; Lima, 2013).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of food chemistry cited from literature

claim: The Maillard reaction has revolutionized the food industry by playing an important role in food chemistry
source: The Maillard reaction has revolutionized the food industry by playing an important role in food chemistry (Machiels and Istasse, 2022); however, this reaction also results in the formation of adverse AGEs as well as toxic byproducts including acrylamide (Luca et al., 2010; Mottram et al., 2022; Stadler et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: The Maillard reaction results in the formation of adverse AGEs as well as toxic byproducts including acrylamide
source: The Maillard reaction has revolutionized the food industry by playing an important role in food chemistry (Machiels and Istasse, 2022); however, this reaction also results in the formation of adverse AGEs as well as toxic byproducts including acrylamide (Luca et al., 2010; Mottram et al., 2022; Stadler et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: AGEs are endogenously produced in cells when α-dicarbonyl compounds non-enzymatically react with biomolecules
source: In addition to food sources, AGEs are also endogenously produced in cells when α-dicarbonyl compounds (α-DCs) (such as glyoxal [GO], methylglyoxal [MGO], and 3-deoxyglucosone [3DG]) non-enzymatically react with biomolecules.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge

claim: α-DCs are unavoidable byproducts of cellular metabolisms, such as glycolysis and lipid peroxidation
source: α-DCs are unavoidable byproducts of cellular metabolisms, such as glycolysis and lipid peroxidation (Figure 1).
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: AGEs include GO derivatives such as carboxymethyl lysine (CML) and glyoxal lysine dimer (GOLD)
source: AGEs include GO derivatives such as carboxymethyl lysine (CML) and glyoxal lysine dimer (GOLD). AGEs derived from MGO include hydroimidazolone (MG-H1), carboxyethyl lysine (CEL), and methylglyoxal lysine dimer (MOLD), and 3DG derivatives include 3-deoxyglucosone-derived imidazolium cross-link (DOGDIC), pyrraline, etc. (Chaudhuri et al., 2018; Allaman et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2018; Vistoli et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: AGEs derived from MGO include hydroimidazolone (MG-H1), carboxyethyl lysine (CEL), and methylglyoxal lysine dimer (MOLD)
source: AGEs include GO derivatives such as carboxymethyl lysine (CML) and glyoxal lysine dimer (GOLD). AGEs derived from MGO include hydroimidazolone (MG-H1), carboxyethyl lysine (CEL), and methylglyoxal lysine dimer (MOLD), and 3DG derivatives include 3-deoxyglucosone-derived imidazolium cross-link (DOGDIC), pyrraline, etc. (Chaudhuri et al., 2018; Allaman et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2018; Vistoli et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: 3DG derivatives include 3-deoxyglucosone-derived imidazolium cross-link (DOGDIC) and pyrraline
source: AGEs include GO derivatives such as carboxymethyl lysine (CML) and glyoxal lysine dimer (GOLD). AGEs derived from MGO include hydroimidazolone (MG-H1), carboxyethyl lysine (CEL), and methylglyoxal lysine dimer (MOLD), and 3DG derivatives include 3-deoxyglucosone-derived imidazolium cross-link (DOGDIC), pyrraline, etc. (Chaudhuri et al., 2018; Allaman et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2018; Vistoli et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: The glyoxalase system utilizes enzymes Glo1 and Glo2 and reduced glutathione (GSH) to detoxify α-DCs stress, especially MGO to lactate
source: The glyoxalase system utilizes enzymes Glo1 and Glo2 and reduced glutathione (GSH) to detoxify α-DCs stress, especially MGO to lactate (Figure 1), in cytosol and nucleus.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: Differential expression levels of glyoxalases are reported in various disease conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, neurodegenerative disorders, anxiety disorders, infertility, and cancer
source: Differential expression levels of glyoxalases are reported in various disease conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, neurodegenerative disorders, anxiety disorders, infertility, and cancer, suggesting their role in exacerbating their pathogenesis (He et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on literature review cited from He et al., 2020

claim: Glo1 has been linked with several behavioral phenotypes, such as anxiety, depression, autism, and pain, among other mental illnesses
source: Glo1 has been linked with several behavioral phenotypes, such as anxiety, depression, autism, and pain, among other mental illnesses (Distler and Palmer, 2012).
evidence: Based on literature review cited from Distler and Palmer, 2012

claim: AGEs accumulate in long-lived proteins, such as collagen
source: AGEs accumulate in long-lived proteins, such as collagen (Monnier et al., 1984); furthermore, quantifying the glycated form of hemoglobin (HbA1c) is utilized as a biomarker in diabetes (Rahbar et al., 1969).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: Quantifying the glycated form of hemoglobin (HbA1c) is utilized as a biomarker in diabetes
source: AGEs accumulate in long-lived proteins, such as collagen (Monnier et al., 1984); furthermore, quantifying the glycated form of hemoglobin (HbA1c) is utilized as a biomarker in diabetes (Rahbar et al., 1969).
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge cited from literature

claim: Increased AGEs are associated with aging, obesity, diabetes, neurodegeneration, inflammation, cardiomyopathy, nephropathy, and other age-related diseases
source: Increased AGEs are associated with aging, obesity, diabetes, neurodegeneration, inflammation, cardiomyopathy, nephropathy, and other age-related diseases (Chaudhuri et al., 2018; Ramasamy et al., 2005; Prasad et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on literature review cited from multiple sources

claim: Neurodegenerative diseases have demonstrated a strong correlation between increased levels of AGEs and pathogenesis
source: Furthermore, neurodegenerative diseases have also demonstrated a strong correlation between increased levels of AGEs and pathogenesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from literature

claim: Overconsumption of food and excessive availability of cheap, highly processed foods have contributed to the obesity pandemic
source: Overconsumption of food and excessive availability of cheap, highly processed foods have contributed to the obesity pandemic.
evidence: Based on established public health knowledge

claim: Obesity is a key risk factor for diabetes, hypertension, cancers, cardiovascular, inflammatory, and neurodegenerative disorders, among other non-communicable chronic diseases
source: Obesity is a key risk factor for other diseases including diabetes, hypertension, cancers, cardiovascular, inflammatory, and neurodegenerative disorders, among other non-communicable chronic diseases (Lee and Yau, 2020; Miller and Spencer, 2014; Wolin et al., 2010; Ellulu et al., 2017; Keramat et al., 2021; Uribarri et al., 2015; Ruhm, 2012; Hossain et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from multiple literature sources

claim: Loss of the glyoxalase system increases food intake in C. elegans
source: Here, we report that loss of the glyoxalase system or exogenously feeding MGO-derived AGEs increased feeding behavior in C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: Exogenously feeding MGO-derived AGEs increases feeding behavior in C. elegans
source: Here, we report that loss of the glyoxalase system or exogenously feeding MGO-derived AGEs increased feeding behavior in C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: This study is the first to identify the signaling pathway mediated by specific AGEs molecules downstream of MGO (such as MG-H1) to enhance feeding and neurodegeneration
source: This study is the first to identify the signaling pathway mediated by specific AGEs molecules downstream of MGO (such as MG-H1) to enhance feeding and neurodegeneration.
evidence: Claim of novelty based on literature review

claim: AGEs accumulation is deleterious and enhances disease pathology in different conditions, including obesity and neurodegeneration
source: Our study emphasizes that AGEs accumulation is deleterious and enhances disease pathology in different conditions, including obesity and neurodegeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings and literature context

claim: Limiting AGEs accumulation is relevant to the global increase in obesity and other age-associated diseases
source: Hence, limiting AGEs accumulation is relevant to the global increase in obesity and other age-associated diseases.
evidence: Speculative statement about implications of the findings

claim: Processed modern diets enriched with AGEs are tempting to eat but deleterious for health
source: Processed modern diets enriched with advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), formed by the Maillard reaction, are tempting to eat but at the same time deleterious for health (Chaudhuri et al., 2018; Nowotny et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on literature review cited from multiple sources

claim: MGO treatment did not change the pumping rate in C. elegans
source: As previously reported by Ravichandran et al., 2018, MGO treatment did not change the pumping rate; however, MG-H1 and CEL increased the pumping rate in wildtype N2 worms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Ravichandran et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and consistent with cited literature

claim: Treatment with sugar-derived AGE-modified bovine serum albumin accelerates the pharyngeal pumping rate
source: Furthermore, a recent study demonstrated that treatment with sugar-derived AGE-modified bovine serum albumin accelerated the pharyngeal pumping rate (Papaevgeniou et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on cited literature

claim: MG-H1-induced hyper-feeding is independent of serotonin-mediated hyper-feeding in C. elegans
source: We also found that MG-H1-induced hyper-feeding is independent of serotonin-mediated hyper-feeding (Dallière et al., 2017) in C. elegans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D and cited literature

claim: AGEs are formed during cooking, browning the food during dry heating, making the food more appetizing
source: It is well established that AGEs are formed during cooking, browning the food during dry heating, making the food more appetizing (Vistoli et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: Feeding is a multisensorial process regulated by several signaling pathways subjected to evolutionary adaptations
source: Furthermore, feeding is a multisensorial process regulated by several signaling pathways subjected to evolutionary adaptations (Luca et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: Tryptophan and tyrosine are the substrates for synthesizing biogenic amines implicated in modulating various behaviors in C. elegans
source: Tryptophan and tyrosine are the substrates for synthesizing biogenic amines implicated in modulating various behaviors in C. elegans (Chase and Koelle, 2007; Alkema et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: Tyrosine to tyramine conversion occurs in the presence of the enzyme tyrosine decarboxylase (TDC-1)
source: Tyrosine to tyramine conversion in the presence of the enzyme tyrosine decarboxylase (TDC-1) followed by tyramine β-hydroxylase (TBH-1), is crucial for the synthesis of neurotransmitters tyramine and octopamine, respectively (Alkema et al., 2005; Greer et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge cited from literature

claim: Tyramine β-hydroxylase (TBH-1) converts tyramine to octopamine
source: Tyrosine to tyramine conversion in the presence of the enzyme tyrosine decarboxylase (TDC-1) followed by tyramine β-hydroxylase (TBH-1), is crucial for the synthesis of neurotransmitters tyramine and octopamine, respectively (Alkema et al., 2005; Greer et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge cited from literature

claim: Previous studies have shown the role of tyramine and its receptor (ser-2) in regulating feeding and foraging behavior in C. elegans
source: Previous studies have shown the role of tyramine and its receptor (ser-2) in regulating feeding and foraging behavior in C. elegans (Dallière et al., 2017; Greer et al., 2008; Rex et al., 2004; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on literature review cited from multiple sources

claim: The tyra-2 receptor is expressed in MC (Marginal Cell) and NSM (NeuroSecretory Motor) pharyngeal neurons
source: Furthermore, the tyra-2 receptor is expressed in MC (Marginal Cell) and NSM (NeuroSecretory Motor) pharyngeal neurons and is discussed to regulate pharyngeal pumping potentially (Dallière et al., 2017; Rex et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: Only two interneurons, RIM (Ring Interneuron M) and RIC (Ring Interneuron C) neurons, uv1 cells near vulva and gonadal sheath cells express the tdc-1 gene
source: It is to be noted that only two interneurons, namely RIM (Ring Interneuron M) and RIC (Ring Interneuron C) neurons, uv1 cells near vulva and gonadal sheath cells (Alkema et al., 2005) express the tdc-1 gene, which is involved in the biosynthesis of tyramine; however, receptors of tyramine are expressed in distant tissues explaining an endocrine activity for tyramine neurotransmitter (Dallière et al., 2017) leading to the multi-pathway mode of action to exert differential response which should be elucidated in the future.
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: Receptors of tyramine are expressed in distant tissues explaining an endocrine activity for tyramine neurotransmitter
source: It is to be noted that only two interneurons, namely RIM (Ring Interneuron M) and RIC (Ring Interneuron C) neurons, uv1 cells near vulva and gonadal sheath cells (Alkema et al., 2005) express the tdc-1 gene, which is involved in the biosynthesis of tyramine; however, receptors of tyramine are expressed in distant tissues explaining an endocrine activity for tyramine neurotransmitter (Dallière et al., 2017) leading to the multi-pathway mode of action to exert differential response which should be elucidated in the future.
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature with speculation about future research

claim: ser-3 is a receptor for octopamine
source: Since ser-3 mutant worms did not suppress the pumping (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) and ser-3 has been demonstrated to be a receptor for octopamine (Dallière et al., 2017), we conclude that octopamine is not responsible for mediating MG-H1-induced feeding in C. elegans.
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: Octopamine is not responsible for mediating MG-H1-induced feeding in C. elegans
source: Since ser-3 mutant worms did not suppress the pumping (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) and ser-3 has been demonstrated to be a receptor for octopamine (Dallière et al., 2017), we conclude that octopamine is not responsible for mediating MG-H1-induced feeding in C. elegans.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing ser-3 mutants do not suppress pumping and knowledge of ser-3 function

claim: elt-3 TF is predominantly expressed in hypodermal cells
source: Although elt-3 TF is predominantly expressed in hypodermal cells, its expression is also reported in the pharyngeal–intestinal valve, intestine, a few neurons (head neurons and mechanosensory PVD (Posterior Ventral process D) neuron), etc. (Wormbase.org).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from Wormbase database

claim: elt-3 expression is also reported in the pharyngeal–intestinal valve, intestine, and a few neurons including head neurons and mechanosensory PVD neuron
source: Although elt-3 TF is predominantly expressed in hypodermal cells, its expression is also reported in the pharyngeal–intestinal valve, intestine, a few neurons (head neurons and mechanosensory PVD (Posterior Ventral process D) neuron), etc. (Wormbase.org).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from Wormbase database

claim: tyra-2 is expressed in PVD neurons
source: In accordance with elt-3 expression in PVD neurons and head neurons, tyra-2 is also expressed in PVD neurons (Rex et al., 2005) and tdc-1 in RIM and RIC head interneurons, respectively, suggesting a possible direct/partial regulation of tdc-1 expression by elt-3.
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature

claim: tdc-1 is expressed in RIM and RIC head interneurons
source: In accordance with elt-3 expression in PVD neurons and head neurons, tyra-2 is also expressed in PVD neurons (Rex et al., 2005) and tdc-1 in RIM and RIC head interneurons, respectively, suggesting a possible direct/partial regulation of tdc-1 expression by elt-3.
evidence: Based on established knowledge with inference about regulation

claim: tyra-2 is expressed in pharyngeal MC neurons, which directly regulate pharyngeal pumping
source: Also, tyra-2 expression has been reported in pharyngeal MC neurons, which directly regulate pharyngeal pumping (Rex et al., 2005), suggesting direct endocrine action of tyramine.
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from literature with inference about endocrine action

claim: ser-2 is expressed in pharyngeal muscle segment cells
source: Similarly, ser-2 is expressed in pharyngeal muscle segment cells (Rex et al., 2004; Li et al., 2012; Tsalik et al., 2003).

claim: Increased expression of ser-2 in elt-3 mutant worms can be inferred as a compensatory mechanism for reduced tyramine signaling
source: Increased expression of ser-2 in elt-3 mutant worms can be inferred as a compensatory mechanism for reduced tyramine signaling by increasing the expression of the tyramine receptor.
evidence: Speculative inference from experimental observation

claim: The ser-2 gene is upregulated in the glod-4 knockdown RNAseq dataset
source: Finally, it is essential to note that the ser-2 gene is upregulated in the glod-4 knockdown RNAseq dataset, similar to significant upregulation after MG-H1 treatment, validating that MG-H1 is a critical player in mediating adverse phenotypes observed in glod-4 mutant worms.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data and qPCR data after MG-H1 treatment

claim: The mechanism behind the behavioral switch from tyramine suppressing pumping in wildtype to stimulating in glod-4 mutant background remains elusive
source: The mechanism behind this behavioral switch, that is, from suppressor of pharyngeal pumping in wildtype to a stimulator in glod-4 mutant background, remains elusive.
evidence: Acknowledgment of unknown mechanism

claim: MG-H1 can modify the tissue-specific expression of tyramine receptors, potentially resulting in the observed behavioral switch in response to tyramine signaling
source: It can be speculated that MG-H1 can modify the tissue-specific expression of tyramine receptors (Figure 4F), resulting in an observed behavioral switch in response to tyramine signaling.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on gene expression data

claim: MG-H1 modifies tyramine signaling by modulating genes in the tyramine pathway, leading to an increased feeding rate in C. elegans
source: Thus, our current understanding is that MG-H1 (either exogenous or endogenous accumulation in glod-4 KO) modifies tyramine signaling by modulating genes in the tyramine pathway, leading to an increased feeding rate in C. elegans.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental findings
